I'm not so sure, I would think the entry level jobs will stay since they are cheap, relatively speaking, for the employer. The entrenched guys and gals who have a fairly high salary - again relatively speaking - are the ones that will be on the chopping block if they can be, because a lot of them are not actually that productive. They do have knowledge that is needed for the business to function, but most of that can be had mining their work email account - which is company property and thus fair game. 
The entry level jobs actually do things AI can't do - they walk around, interact with people etc, to my mind there may be a situation where a company might hire a person as a form of assistant or agent for an AI - a form of "interface" as it were. I used to work as a software dev and a fair bit of what I ended up doing was acting as a kind of interface between the systems I built and maintained, and the people who used them on a basic level. So people would have to explain to me properly what they wanted the system to do, and I would either explain to them how to do get the system to do what they wanted, or I would build the functionality they wanted when it was missing and then explain to them how I set it up for them to be able to do what it is they wanted to. There was a bunch of "translation work" needed, because business people are often 'process illiterate' in the sense that they don't understand that you need to have clearly defined criteria to base a decision to do X instead of Y on. You can't have "the customer might be of a type that needs to have things done according to procedure B instead of A that most have" - there has to be a defined criterion for choosing B instead of A, it doesn't make sense to just pick one or the other based on gut-feel. In what I did it often was tied to someone being an individual private customer VS them being a reseller for example, or them being an educational institute, or in some cases banks and such have a particular way of working that requires a different "journey" for the lack of a better way to explain it, to get from A to B for a set specific task, than others do. 
But anyway, that is how I see some of this stuff going, when I started at one point working on a system we had 2 guys doing a specific task all day every day, then one of them left, and we simply never replaced him, the system had sufficient automation that there was no need for a replacement, the little that was left was basically split and part of that task was sent to the individuals who worked as agents for the system in a sense.. But that also became less and less as the automation got better as well as we had new options we could use which I built logic in to select instead of it becoming a manual process. A couple of years down the line the one guy who was left was complaining that he had very little to do because a lot of what he used to do manually was automated and pushed "down in the hierarchy" and successfully enough that almost nothing reached him. He then had an accident and was out for a couple of months I think - during which time to keep things going some of the decisionmaking was further automated in terms of latitude as well - and when he came back there was nothing much left for him to do. I think he ended up leaving - I had a heart attack and then not much later broke my back etc and medically retired, and it seems I was not replaced. A "token tax" on AI companies would almost certainly be structured as a cost-per-API-call or per-computational-unit fee, which creates a regressive burden that falls heaviest on exactly the people who can least afford it - students, researchers, small businesses, individual developers, displaced workers, and startups.
The demographic most disenfranchised would be those without institutional backing or deep pockets. A major corporation can absorb token taxes as a minor cost of doing business, but an independent researcher, a student working on a thesis project, or someone trying to build a small application would be priced out entirely.
      
It's the classic pattern - a policy ostensibly designed to address systemic problems (job displacement from AI) ends up reinforcing the very power structures that created those problems. Large tech companies get to maintain their oligopoly position while smaller players get eliminated from the market.
     
The irony is particularly sharp given that Amodei is positioning this as a solution to AI-induced unemployment. But the token tax would accelerate the concentration of AI capabilities in the hands of the few companies wealthy enough to pay it, making the job displacement problem worse rather than better.
      
It's like proposing to solve wealth inequality by implementing a tax that only rich people can afford to pay - it achieves the opposite of its stated goal while creating a convenient revenue stream for the very entities causing the original problem.
       
The people who would benefit most from democratized AI access - those who might use it to create new opportunities or compete with established players - are precisely the ones who would be locked out.
